_about: InsightsOut findings ledger. Single source of truth for every published number. Papers and pages reference findings by id via data-finding attributes; never hard-code a stat in HTML. Numbers seeded 2026-08-18 from 'Workshop Themed Findings 2026-08' (9 waves, 444 registrations, 363 unique people, Mar-Jul 2026) and hypothesis-status. Re-verify against the master dataset before each edition.

dataset.limits: Registration-time answers (needs and intent, not outcomes); self-selected, San Francisco / startup-ecosystem heavy; questionnaire varied by event so cross-event counts use a conservative theme mapping; role not captured at OTF and FIC.

findings.claim: Roughly half of respondents describe their hardest problem as uncertainty or lack of clarity about what to decide next — across every event and every segment.

anchor.note: Organizational factors (culture, manager support, talent practices) drive about twice the AI-value impact of individual factors — the bottleneck is not individual knowledge.

findings.claim: When asked what they want to walk out with, the top picks are a strategy to choose and a way to move fast without chaos — not tool training.

stat.detail: 'knowing what strategy to choose' 31/73; 'moving fast without chaos' 25/73

findings.claim: Time, focus, and prioritization is the #1 free-text challenge, but people describe fragmentation ('many hats, no filter') — not a shortage of hours.

stat.detail: top free-text challenge, OTF

anchor.source: MIT Sloan Management Review, 'When Employees Are Drowning in Change'
anchor.note: Change fatigue framed as an organizational-load problem, not individual resilience.

findings.claim: On the same form, non-founders name lack of trust in leadership far more often than founders do.

stat.detail: non-founders vs founders, ROLE form

anchor.source: SHRM, Navigating AI in the Workplace 2026
anchor.note: Only 47% of individual contributors trust leadership on AI vs 80% of directors.

findings.claim: Managers are the only large segment where relational pain — trust, resistance, communication — is named by a majority.

stat.detail: managers vs under 50% for every other segment

anchor.source: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2026
anchor.note: Gallup reports manager engagement falling ~3x faster than employees'. In our rooms managers are not disengaged — they are overloaded and silent. Different diagnosis, different fix.

findings.claim: Only about a third of emotion answers are exclusively heavy; the modal pattern pairs excited/curious with overwhelmed/uncertain.

stat.detail: 38 of 121 exclusively heavy

anchor.source: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2026 ('the human side of the AI revolution')
anchor.note: Contradicts the standard 'overcoming resistance' change-management frame.

findings.claim: Peer conversation is the most-requested form of support, ahead of content or tools.

stat.detail: top non-Other support pick, ROLE form

anchor.note: External literature is thin here — a differentiated finding.

findings.claim: Founders and executives ask for strategy; ICs, managers, and people in transition ask for clearer communication and leadership alignment — the same gap, seen from opposite sides.

stat.detail: 'clearer communication' 50/163, 'better leadership alignment' 35/163 among non-founders

anchor.note: Candidate finding — one form so far. Needs a second wave before it carries a headline.

findings.claim: Asked where the change is felt most, more than one in five people navigating role change point to their identity or sense of value — not their workload.

stat.detail: 'my identity or sense of value', ROLE form

anchor.source: SHRM, Navigating AI in the Workplace 2026
anchor.note: 27% of early-career workers fear AI will devalue their field; 45% of workers overall expect to reskill.

findings.claim: AI adoption is the single most-named kind of change people are navigating.

stat.detail: top 'kind of change', ROLE form

findings.claim: Among people who describe themselves as in career or role transition, uncertainty about direction is close to universal.

stat.detail: of 23 self-described in-transition respondents; managers 62%, startup operators 63%, founders 45%

anchor.source: Anthropic, What 81,000 people told us about the economics of AI (Apr 2026)
anchor.note: Early-career workers report substantially higher displacement concern than senior professionals.

findings.claim: Fear or anxiety about the change is named roughly three times as often by individual contributors and people in transition as by founders.

stat.detail: product/eng ICs 33% (n=21), in transition 39% (n=23), founders 11% (n=141); on the identical ROLE form: 32% non-founders vs 27% founders

anchor.source: Anthropic, What 81,000 people told us about the economics of AI (Apr 2026)
anchor.note: Displacement concern is highest where role security is lowest.

findings.claim: A map of what skills or capacities to build next is the #1 thing people navigating role change want to leave with — even though almost nobody names a skill gap as their biggest pain.

stat.detail: #1 desired outcome, ROLE form; skill gap named as a pain by only 9% across the dataset

anchor.source: SHRM, Navigating AI in the Workplace 2026
anchor.note: The field talks about reskilling as courses; people ask for a map, not a curriculum.

findings.claim: People want a practical next step and peer conversation in almost equal measure — and say the peer part must not feel like networking.

stat.detail: 'a practical next step' 53, 'peer conversations with others navigating change' 52, 'practical decision-making tools' 37

findings.claim: Asked to pick two emotions, founders paired an activating one with a heavy one: curious and uncertain, energized and anxious.

stat.detail: OTC founders, pick 2 of 10; Overwhelmed 11, Hopeful 11, Lonely 7, Stuck 7

findings.claim: On the identical form, non-founders name communication breakdown and leader–team misalignment two to four times as often as founders.

stat.detail: communication breakdown; misalignment between leaders and teams — non-founders (n=108) vs founders (n=55)

anchor.source: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2026
anchor.note: Employees whose managers champion AI are 8.7x more likely to report AI transforming their work — the manager is the transmission line.

findings.claim: Three quarters of the founders in our rooms are pre-revenue: building an MVP, exploring an idea, or launched without revenue.

stat.detail: Building MVP 53 · Idea/exploring 38 · Launched pre-revenue 37 · Early revenue 23 · Post-revenue 14 · Fundraising 9 · Funded/scaling 7 (of 170 who gave a stage)

anchor.note: This is an early-stage room. Almost nobody is scaling a team.

findings.claim: When founders write their main challenge in their own words, money and customers come first — often before any human theme.

stat.detail: funding/capital 15, customers/GTM/traction 16, co-founder/hiring/team 12 of 120 free-text answers

findings.claim: Founders almost never call it 'decision fatigue' — but a third pick 'moving fast without creating chaos'. Same load, different word.

stat.detail: 'decision fatigue' named by 5% of founders (n=141); 'moving fast without creating chaos' picked by 25 of 73 and 'knowing what strategy to choose' by 31 of 73 (OTF)

anchor.source: Bloomberg, 'AI Anxiety Is Fueling Burnout Across Silicon Valley's Tech Workers' (June 2026)
anchor.note: Bloomberg documents founders working longer, not less, as AI raises the bar. Our founders describe the same pressure as pace and strategy, not exhaustion.

findings.claim: Nearly half of founders name uncertainty or lack of clarity about direction as their hardest thing — the one theme they share with everyone else in the room.

stat.detail: of 141 founders who answered a pain question; on the identical ROLE form founders name raw uncertainty more than non-founders (55% vs 48%)

findings.claim: Solo founders and co-founders are both in the room; the solo ones describe being the single point of failure on everything.

stat.detail: of 49 who answered (OTC); free text repeats 'solo founder with no team', 'single point of failure on fundraising, product, and recruiting'

findings.claim: Loneliness is quiet in the structured answers and loud in what draws founders to the smaller circles: safe space and non-performative peer community.

stat.detail: FIC 'what drew you' answers about community / safe space; 'lonely' picked 7 times as an emotion (OTC); 'loneliness at the top' 4

anchor.note: Directional. Consistent, small, and only asked directly once.

findings.claim: Founders name fear about one time in nine — roughly a third the rate of the people who work for them.

stat.detail: founders (n=141) vs product/eng ICs 33%, in transition 39%; on the identical ROLE form 27% vs 32%

anchor.note: Whether founders feel it less or report it less is not knowable from this data.

findings.claim: Coaching interest is real but lukewarm; when founders say yes, they want a group or circle at least as much as one-to-one — and almost nobody asks for a workshop for their team.

stat.detail: Yes 97, Maybe 84, Not right now 55 of 236; among Yes: group/circle ≈ 1:1 > team workshop (20 across all events)

anchor.source: ManpowerGroup / Everest Group, The New Talent Equation (July 2026)
anchor.note: Only 3% of organizations say their leaders are ready to lead AI-enabled teams — yet the demand for team-level help does not come from the people in our rooms. It has to be brought to leaders, not pulled by them.
